claims.text: The degree of atomic or chemical disorder primarily governs superconducting behavior in high-entropy alloys.
Atomic or chemical disorder governs superconductivity by modulating electron–phonon coupling strength.
Annealing can reduce atomic or chemical disorder while leaving the overall alloy composition constant.
The as-cast near-equiatomic HEA has high atomic disorder.
Chemical short-range order modifies the phonon density of states, particularly its high-frequency portion.
Reducing disorder sharpens the phonon density of states.
Lower disorder promotes more coherent vibrational modes.
More coherent vibrational modes enhance electron–phonon coupling strength.
Stronger electron–phonon coupling facilitates Cooper-pair formation and raises the superconducting transition temperature.
Annealed samples with reduced disorder will have a higher superconducting transition temperature than as-cast samples.
Annealed samples will have a larger electron–phonon coupling constant than as-cast samples.
Annealing-induced disorder reduction will produce a shift or sharpening of the phonon density of states.
The electron–phonon coupling constant can be quantified through tunneling spectroscopy or specific-heat analysis.
The proposed mechanism is limited to near-equiatomic HEAs in which synthesis changes atomic-scale disorder appreciably.
The proposed relationship may fail when superconductivity is dominated by electronic density-of-states variations unrelated to disorder.
A controlled as-cast versus annealed comparison at constant composition can isolate the effect of disorder.

Failure to observe the predicted increases in transition temperature and electron–phonon coupling, or failure to observe the predicted phonon-density-of-states modification, would falsify the hypothesis.
